rv.q: That “44” manages to pull off a feel-good tone in the context of today’s political headlines is impressive: It’s a love letter to the Obamas tucked inside the envelope of a “Saturday Night Live” sketch that, against all odds, aims to deliver uncomplicated fun.
I was less ecstatic. Not so much because of '44''s content, although the reviews have been mixed, as because of its existence.
The show may not have my vote, but I must concede that it seems to poll better with others.
The result is a show that feels mounted ten years too late.
44: The Musical's satirical take on former President Barack Obama falters with repetitive music, scattershot humor, and a thin point of view.
Eli Bauman's musical mistakes vulgarity for actual entertainment, with a hard-working cast vainly trying
Those who like sophisticated entertainments are better off staying away.
By mixing sharp satire with moments of sincerity, Bauman has created something rare: a political parody with guts, groin, and heart.

It’s a playful, buoyant romp through recent history—part memory, part myth, part musical revue—and it delivers what it promises: a good-spirited, sharply performed evening of political theater that delights far more than it debates.

cn.t: Critics are split on "44: The Musical" — some find its profanity-laced Obama satire a feel-good crowd-pleaser with a strong cast, while others call it tonally confused and mistake vulgarity for wit.

vr.q: If all of this sounds like really ridiculously fun to you, then this is the show for you.
